directAnswer: St. Stephen I was the twenty-third bishop of Rome, from 254 to 257. He is best known for his dispute with St. Cyprian of Carthage over baptism administered by heretics: Stephen held that such baptisms were valid and should not be repeated, a position the Church later confirmed. Tradition says he was beheaded in the persecution of Valerian, though early sources do not clearly support this.

paras: In North Africa and parts of Asia Minor, converts from heretical or schismatic groups such as the Novatianists were baptized again, because those churches held that baptism outside the Catholic Church was invalid. Rome followed an older custom of receiving such converts by the laying on of hands for penance, without repeating baptism.

Cyprian and synods in Carthage defended rebaptism and wrote to Stephen. According to Cyprian, Stephen insisted that nothing should be innovated beyond what had been handed down, and he threatened to break communion with those who rebaptized. Firmilian, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, sided with Cyprian and wrote a harsh letter against Stephen that survives among Cyprian’s correspondence.

Stephen’s pontificate also shows Rome being drawn into other churches’ affairs. Cyprian urged him to act against Marcian, bishop of Arles, who had joined the Novatianist position and refused reconciliation to the repentant. Two Spanish bishops, Basilides and Martial, who had been deposed for lapsing, appealed to Stephen and were restored, prompting the Spanish churches to seek Cyprian’s advice instead.
These episodes reveal a bishop of Rome who saw himself as having responsibility beyond his city, and other bishops who did not always agree with how he used it.

The dispute was not resolved during Stephen’s lifetime, and peace between Rome and Carthage was restored under his successor, Sixtus II. In the following century, the Council of Arles in 314 and later theology, especially that of St. Augustine, affirmed Stephen’s principle that baptism given with water in the name of the Trinity is valid even when performed by heretics, and so must not be repeated.
This remains Catholic teaching today and is why the Church recognizes the baptisms of many other Christian communities.

A later legend says Stephen was beheaded while seated on his episcopal chair in the catacombs during the persecution of Valerian. Many historians think this story was borrowed from the martyrdom of his successor, Sixtus II, since the Liberian Catalogue and the earliest Roman calendars do not list Stephen as a martyr.
His resting place was the crypt of the popes in the Catacomb of St. Callixtus, and the Church keeps his feast on August 2.

keyFacts: Twenty-third bishop of Rome, May 12, 254, to August 2, 257
Taught that baptism given by heretics is valid and must not be repeated
Clashed with St. Cyprian of Carthage and Firmilian of Caesarea
Received appeals from bishops in Spain and concerns about Arles in Gaul
Martyrdom by beheading is a later tradition; buried in the papal crypt of St. Callixtus

faqs.question: What was the rebaptism controversy?
faqs.answer: It was a dispute over whether converts baptized in heretical or schismatic groups needed to be baptized again. St. Cyprian said yes; Pope Stephen I said no, holding that a baptism given properly in the name of the Trinity is valid. The Church later adopted Stephen’s view.

faqs.question: Was Pope Stephen I really beheaded on his chair?
faqs.answer: That is a later tradition. Several early Roman lists do not call him a martyr, and historians suspect the story was transferred from Pope Sixtus II, who was executed in the catacombs in 258.

faqs.question: Did Pope Stephen I and St. Cyprian ever reconcile?
faqs.answer: Not during Stephen’s life. Peace was restored under his successor, Sixtus II, and both Stephen and Cyprian are honored as saints.
